title: Bhageeratha
body:
Bhageeratha

Bhageeratha belonged to the illustrious Ikshvaku dynasty and was an ancestor of Lord Rama, a man of unwavering resolve who bore upon his shoulders a responsibility no one before him had been able to fulfill — the liberation of his ancestors. To understand his task one must first know the sorrow of his line. Long ago King Sagara had performed the Ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice by which a king asserts his sovereignty. Indra, in fear and envy, stole the ceremonial horse and hid it near the hermitage of the great sage Kapila. When Sagara's sixty thousand sons traced the horse to the hermitage, they stormed in without reverence and disturbed the sage's deep meditation. Kapila, an incarnation of Sriman Narayana whose very glance can burn away ignorance, opened his eyes in displeasure, and in that instant all sixty thousand were reduced to ash.
Only through the descent of the celestial river Ganga upon their remains could their souls find peace, and generation after generation of the Sagara line tried to bring her down from the heavens, all in vain. Then came Bhageeratha. He renounced his throne and its comforts and stood in penance so severe that it shook the very foundations of existence; the seasons turned and his body wasted, yet his mind never left its goal. At last Brahma appeared and asked what he sought, and Bhageeratha answered that he desired neither wealth nor power nor dominion, but only that Mother Ganga descend to the earth so that his ancestors might be freed. Brahma granted the wish, but warned that the force of Ganga's fall was beyond the earth to bear — unchecked, she would shatter the very land; only one being could receive her.
Bhageeratha knew who that was, and he began his penance anew, this time meditating upon Lord Shiva, the only one capable of catching the descent of the celestial river. When Shiva at last appeared, He agreed to receive Ganga upon His head, but told the king that it fell to him to lead her onward to his ancestors. And so Ganga began her descent, proud and untamed, roaring down with the force of a thousand storms, seeking to sweep all before her. But the moment she touched Shiva's matted locks He tightened them, capturing her within an endless labyrinth, and not a single drop reached the earth. At Bhageeratha's humble plea, Shiva released a single stream, and Ganga flowed forth onto the Himalayas as the most sacred of rivers.
Bhageeratha walked before her, guiding her course toward the place where his ancestors lay in ash. But as she flowed she destroyed the hermitage of a sage named Jahnu, who in his anger drew upon his penance and swallowed the entire river. Bhageeratha went to Jahnu and appealed to him, recounting all the struggles he had endured to liberate his ancestors, and the sage relented and released Ganga from his ear. As the sacred waters at last touched the ashes of the sixty thousand, their souls rose, freed at last and carried to liberation. Because she was brought down by Bhageeratha, Ganga came to be known as Bhagirathi, and because she was released by Jahnu, she came also to be called Jahnavi. His name endures not because he ruled, but because through sheer devotion and perseverance he brought the divine to the mortal realm, giving the land its holiest river, whose waters still wash away the burdens of all who seek her.
